chapter.name: Electrostatic Potential and Capacitance
chapter.blurb: Because the electrostatic force is conservative, every point in a field can be given a potential, and the chapter builds this idea up from a point charge to a dipole and a system of charges, linking it to the field through equipotential surfaces and to the energy of charges and dipoles. It then turns to conductors and dielectrics in electrostatic fields and to capacitors: the parallel plate capacitor with and without a dielectric, series and parallel combinations, and the energy a capacitor stores in its electric field.

scope_in.item: State that the Coulomb force is conservative; define potential energy difference as the work done by an external force (equal and opposite to the electric force) in moving a charge without acceleration, W_RP = U_P - U_R; explain why only differences matter and why the zero is chosen at infinity
Define electrostatic potential as work done per unit positive charge in bringing a charge from infinity; use W = q(V_P - V_R); unit volt
Use V = Q/(4 pi epsilon0 r) for a point charge, including the sign of V for Q < 0 and the 1/r variation of V against the 1/r^2 variation of E (Example 2.1)

Use the dipole potential V = p cos(theta)/(4 pi epsilon0 r^2) for r >> a: +p/(4 pi epsilon0 r^2) or -p/(4 pi epsilon0 r^2) on the axis, zero in the equatorial plane; contrast it with the potential of a single charge (angle dependence, 1/r^2 fall-off)

Find the potential of a system of point charges by algebraic superposition, including points of zero potential on the line joining two charges (Example 2.2, Exercises 2.1-2.2); potential outside and inside a uniformly charged spherical shell
Decide signs of potential difference, potential energy difference and work for charges moved near a positive or negative point charge (Example 2.3)

Describe equipotential surfaces (concentric spheres for a point charge, planes normal to a uniform field, the equatorial plane of a dipole) and explain why the field is normal to them and no work is done on them (Exercise 2.3)
Relate field and potential: the field points in the direction of steepest decrease of potential and |E| = |delta V|/delta l normal to the equipotential surface; apply to uniform fields

Calculate the potential energy of two and of three or more point charges as a sum over pairs, U = q1 q2/(4 pi epsilon0 r12) + ..., with signs, and the work to assemble or separate a configuration; independence of the order of assembly (Example 2.4)
Use U = qV(r) for a charge in an external field; the electron volt and its multiples; U = q1 V(r1) + q2 V(r2) + q1 q2/(4 pi epsilon0 r12) for two charges in an external field (Example 2.5)

Potential energy of a dipole in a uniform field: work by an external torque pE(cos theta0 - cos theta1), U = -pE cos(theta) = -p.E with zero at 90 degrees, and its origin from the two-charge expression (Example 2.6)

State and justify the electrostatic properties of conductors: zero field inside, field normal to the surface, no excess charge in the interior, constant potential, E = sigma/epsilon0 at the surface (pill-box derivation), and electrostatic shielding of a charge-free cavity; everyday cases of Example 2.7 (Exercise 2.4)

Describe dielectrics: polar and non-polar molecules, induced and orientational polarisation, polarisation P = epsilon0 chi_e E for linear isotropic dielectrics, bound surface charges and the reduction (not cancellation) of the field inside

Define a capacitor and capacitance C = Q/V, the farad and its sub-multiples; explain why C depends only on geometry (and the dielectric), and the role of dielectric strength (about 3 x 10^6 V/m for air) in limiting the charge stored
Derive and use C = epsilon0 A/d for a parallel plate capacitor: field sigma/epsilon0 between the plates and zero outside, fringing, V = Ed, the size of 1 F (Exercise 2.8)

Explain and use the effect of a dielectric filling a capacitor: E = (sigma - sigma_p)/epsilon0 = sigma/(epsilon0 K), C = K epsilon0 A/d = K C0, permittivity epsilon = epsilon0 K, dielectric constant K > 1; a slab filling part of the gap by the method of Example 2.8; supply connected versus disconnected (Exercises 2.5, 2.9)

Find effective capacitance, charges and potential differences for capacitors in series (1/C = 1/C1 + 1/C2 + ...) and in parallel (C = C1 + C2 + ...), and for simple networks (Example 2.9, Exercises 2.6-2.7)

Calculate the energy stored in a capacitor, U = (1/2)QV = (1/2)CV^2 = Q^2/(2C), the energy density (1/2) epsilon0 E^2, and the energy lost when a charged capacitor shares charge with an uncharged one (Example 2.10, Exercises 2.10-2.11)

concepts.name: Electrostatic potential energy, potential and the potential of a point charge
concepts.description: Electrostatic force is conservative, so a charge in a field has potential energy; potential is the work done per unit positive charge by an external force in bringing a charge from infinity, and for a point charge Q it equals Q/(4 pi epsilon0 r).
concepts.idea: Because the work done by the electrostatic field depends only on the end points, each point in a field can be given a potential: the work an external force does per unit positive charge in bringing a charge there from infinity without acceleration.
concepts.rule: Work done by an external force in moving charge q from R to P without acceleration = U_P - U_R = q(V_P - V_R). Only differences are physically significant; with the zero chosen at infinity, a point charge Q gives V(r) = Q/(4 pi epsilon0 r), positive for Q > 0 and negative for Q < 0.
concepts.example: A charge of 4 x 10^-7 C gives a potential of 9 x 10^9 x 4 x 10^-7 / 0.09 = 4 x 10^4 V at a point 9 cm away; bringing 2 x 10^-9 C from infinity to that point needs W = qV = 8 x 10^-5 J, whatever the path.

questions.q: Explain why the concept of electrostatic potential energy would not be meaningful if the work done by an electrostatic field in moving a charge depended on the path taken.
questions.a: Potential energy difference between two points is defined as the work done by the external force (equal and opposite to the electric force) in moving the charge from one point to the other. For this to give one definite value for a given pair of points, the work must depend only on the initial and final positions. If it depended on the path, different paths would give different values and no single potential energy could be assigned to a point. Because the electrostatic force is conservative, the work is path-independent and the definition is meaningful.
s: Potential energy difference is defined through the work done between two points
A unique value needs path-independent work, i.e. a conservative force

questions.a: (a) They disagree about the potential at a point: the second student's value is 50 V higher everywhere. (b) They agree about the work, because work depends only on the potential difference, and (V_P + 50) - (V_R + 50) = V_P - V_R. questions.q: At a certain point the potential due to an isolated point charge is 1800 V (zero at infinity) and the magnitude of its electric field is 6000 N/C. Take 1/(4 pi epsilon0) = 9 x 10^9 N m^2/C^2. Find the distance of the point from the charge and the magnitude of the charge.
questions.a: For a point charge V = Q/(4 pi epsilon0 r) and E = Q/(4 pi epsilon0 r^2), so V/E = r. Hence r = 1800 V / 6000 N/C = 0.30 m. Then Q = V r / (9 x 10^9) = 1800 x 0.30 / (9 x 10^9) = 6 x 10^-8 C. Check: E = 9 x 10^9 x 6 x 10^-8 / (0.30)^2 = 6000 N/C.
s: Uses V/E = r for a point charge

questions.q: A student claims that more work is needed to bring a small charge from infinity to a point P near a fixed point charge along a long curved path than along the straight radial path. Evaluate this claim using the textbook's argument.
questions.a: The claim is wrong: the work is the same for every path. Any small piece of an arbitrary path can be resolved into a displacement along the radial direction r and one perpendicular to r. The electric force is radial, so the work for the perpendicular displacement is zero; only the radial part contributes, and it adds up to the same total for any path between the same end points.
s: States that the work is path-independent, so the claim is wrong
Reason: perpendicular displacements need no work, only the radial part counts

concepts.name: Potential due to an electric dipole and a system of charges
concepts.description: Potential obeys superposition: for a system of charges it is the algebraic sum of the individual potentials, and for a dipole at a far point it is p cos(theta)/(4 pi epsilon0 r^2).
concepts.idea: Potential is a scalar, so the potentials of several charges simply add with their signs. Adding the potentials of +q and -q gives the dipole potential, which depends on direction as well as distance and falls off faster than that of a single charge.
concepts.rule: V = (1/(4 pi epsilon0)) (q1/r1P + q2/r2P + ... + qn/rnP). For a dipole of moment p (r >> a): V = p cos(theta)/(4 pi epsilon0 r^2), i.e. +p/(4 pi epsilon0 r^2) or -p/(4 pi epsilon0 r^2) on the axis and zero in the equatorial plane. For a charged shell of radius R: V = q/(4 pi epsilon0 r) outside, and the constant q/(4 pi epsilon0 R) inside.
concepts.example: For charges 3 x 10^-8 C and -2 x 10^-8 C placed 15 cm apart, the potential is zero where 3/x = 2/(15 - x), i.e. 9 cm from the positive charge, and also where 3/x = 2/(x - 15), i.e. 45 cm from it on the far side of the negative charge.

questions.a: Let the point be at x cm. The potential is zero where 6/r1 = 2/r2, with r1 and r2 the distances from the two charges. Between the charges: 6/x = 2/(20 - x), so 120 - 6x = 2x and x = 15 cm. Beyond the negative charge: 6/x = 2/(x - 20), so 6x - 120 = 2x and x = 30 cm. For x < 0 the point is always nearer the larger charge, so the potentials cannot cancel. The potential is zero at x = 15 cm and x = 30 cm.

x = 15 cm, between the charges

On the far side of the larger charge every point is nearer to the larger charge, so its potential always dominates and the sum cannot be zero.

concepts.name: Equipotential surfaces and the relation between field and potential
concepts.description: An equipotential surface has the same potential at every point; the electric field is everywhere normal to it, points towards decreasing potential, and has magnitude equal to the change in potential per unit normal distance.
concepts.idea: Surfaces of constant potential give a second picture of a field alongside field lines. No work is needed to move a charge along such a surface, so the field can have no component along it.
concepts.rule: The field at a point is normal to the equipotential surface through it, is directed the way the potential decreases most steeply, and has magnitude |E| = |delta V|/delta l, where delta l is the normal distance between two close equipotential surfaces. A point charge has concentric spherical equipotentials; a uniform field has plane equipotentials normal to the field.
concepts.example: In a uniform field of 250 V/m the equipotential planes drawn for every 5 V are 5/250 = 0.02 m = 2 cm apart, and the potential falls by 5 V for every 2 cm moved along the field.

concepts.name: Electrostatics of conductors and electrostatic shielding
concepts.description: In the static situation a conductor has zero field inside, field normal to its surface of magnitude sigma/epsilon0 just outside, excess charge only on its surface and the same potential throughout; a charge-free cavity inside a conductor is shielded from outside fields.
concepts.idea: A conductor has free charge carriers. They keep moving until nothing pushes them any more, and that single requirement fixes the field, the charge distribution and the potential of a conductor in equilibrium.
concepts.rule: Inside a conductor E = 0. At the surface E is normal to the surface, with E = sigma/epsilon0 directed outward for sigma > 0 and inward for sigma < 0. Excess charge resides only on the surface. The potential is constant throughout the volume and on the surface. concepts.name: Dielectrics, polarisation and the effect of a dielectric on capacitance

concepts.idea: A dielectric has no free carriers, but its molecules become (or already are) dipoles that line up with an applied field. Their collective effect is a pair of bound surface charge layers that reduce, but never fully cancel, the field inside.
concepts.rule: Polarisation P (dipole moment per unit volume) = epsilon0 chi_e E for a linear isotropic dielectric. In a filled parallel plate capacitor E = (sigma - sigma_p)/epsilon0 = sigma/(epsilon0 K), so V = Qd/(epsilon0 K A) and C = K epsilon0 A/d = K C0, with K = epsilon/epsilon0 > 1 (K = 1 for vacuum).

concepts.name: Combination of capacitors and energy stored in a capacitor
concepts.description: Capacitors in series share the same charge and add as reciprocals; capacitors in parallel share the same potential difference and add directly; a charged capacitor stores energy (1/2)QV, which can be regarded as stored in the electric field with energy density (1/2) epsilon0 E^2.
concepts.idea: A combination of capacitors can be replaced by one effective capacitor that holds the same charge at the same total potential difference. Charging a capacitor takes work, which is stored as potential energy in the field between the plates.
concepts.rule: Series: same charge Q on each, V = V1 + V2 + ..., 1/C = 1/C1 + 1/C2 + ... . Parallel: same V across each, Q = Q1 + Q2 + ..., C = C1 + C2 + ... . Energy U = (1/2)QV = (1/2)CV^2 = Q^2/(2C); energy density of an electric field u = (1/2) epsilon0 E^2.
concepts.example: A 2 micro-F capacitor charged to 50 V stores (1/2) x 2 x 10^-6 x 50^2 = 2.5 x 10^-3 J; in series with a 3 micro-F capacitor the pair has 1/C = 1/2 + 1/3, i.e. C = 1.2 micro-F.

questions.q: A 2 micro-F capacitor is charged to 300 V and then disconnected from the supply. It is next connected across an uncharged 4 micro-F capacitor. After: U' = (1/2) x 6 x 10^-6 x (100)^2 = 0.03 J. Energies 0.09 J before and 0.03 J after
Loss of 0.06 J as heat and electromagnetic radiation during the transient current
